title: Ashtpadi 3, salok: many scriptures
hook: I have searched many scriptures; none equals the Name (Sukhmani 3)

segments.voice: Yesterday, living the second ashtpadi, and your line: never alone. Did you remember once, just for the company? Today, the third ashtpadi opens with its salok. Day four hundred forty-six.

Think of someone who has read everything. Shelves to the ceiling, notes in every margin, an answer to every question you ask. You can learn a great deal from a person like that. But you've probably also met someone who's read very little and yet carries a kind of steadiness the reader doesn't have. A grandmother who knew three prayers by heart and lived every one of them. Guru Arjan compiled one of the great scriptures of the world. And the third ashtpadi of Sukhmani opens with a surprising thing for a compiler of scripture to say.
screen: `SHELVES TO THE CEILING.` → `A GRANDMOTHER WITH THREE PRAYERS.` → `A COMPILER OF SCRIPTURE SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: Here is the salok: bahu saasatr bahu simritee pekhe sarab dhadhol. Word by word. Bahu: many. Saasatr: the shastras, the learned treatises of Guru Arjan's world. Simritee: the smritis, the remembered law-books and traditions. Pekhe: I have looked at. Sarab dhadhol: searched through them all. Then the second line: poojas naahee har hare, Naanak naam amol. In paraphrase: they do not equal God, Har, Har; Nanak, the Name is priceless. Amol means beyond price, something no amount of money could buy. Notice who is speaking and how. Not someone who dismisses books without opening them. Someone who says, I have looked, I've searched them all. It's the voice of a scholar, not a scorner. And what he found is that the books point beyond themselves. All that learning can describe the Name, but it can't be the Name. Many Sikhs hear the salok this way: it isn't against study. The Guru Granth Sahib is itself a book, and Sikhs read it every day. The salok is about the difference between knowing about God and remembering God. Learning about water is not drinking it. Sikhs read the line as being as true of their own scripture as of any other: a Sikh who reads the Guru Granth Sahib without remembering the One it points to has missed the point too. The salok sets the theme for the whole third ashtpadi. Over the next days its stanzas will run through every great spiritual effort of its time, and set each beside the Name.
screen: `BAHU SAASATR: MANY SCRIPTURES.` · `I HAVE SEARCHED THEM ALL.` · `AMOL: BEYOND PRICE.` · `KNOWING ABOUT VS. REMEMBERING.` · then, large: `NOTHING EQUALS THE NAME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one line slowly. Choose one line you know, from Sukhmani, from Japji, or from anything that matters to you. If nothing comes, use this: Nanak, the Name is priceless. Say it once at normal speed. Then again, at half speed. Then once more, one word per breath. Notice how the line changes when you stop reading about it and start sitting in it. Let the last word rest. If you pray, add Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Ashtpadi 3. Sukhmani's third section, whose salok says: I have searched many shastras and smritis, and none equals God; Nanak, the Name is priceless.
Your line: nothing equals the name. Today, when you read or hear something wise, pause before scrolling on, and let one line of it become something you do. Day four hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: Sikhs reading Sukhmani recite this salok at the start of the third ashtpadi; it is often cited in Sikh teaching on the difference between scholarship and lived remembrance of the Name.

fork.setup: you've searched every learned treatise and law-book of your day. what does the third salok say you find?
options: that none of them equals God, and the Name is priceless.
fork.reveal: bahu saasatr bahu simritee pekhe sarab dhadhol: searched them all, and the Name is amol, beyond price.

original.note: Gurmukhi: amol, priceless; the salok's last word for the Name.

trapdoor: what you thought: many scriptures means reading widely.
what it means: the salok's speaker has searched every shastra and smriti and found that none equals remembering God.
what a scholar hears: saasatr and simritee name the Sanskrit learned and legal corpora; the salok contrasts textual knowledge with naam, without rejecting study.

notes: Salok transliterated 'bahu saasatr bahu simritee pekhe sarab dhadhol / poojas naahee har hare naanak naam amol' with glosses; confirm, especially dhadhol (searched through).
Framing: the salok is presented as about knowing vs remembering, applied by Sikhs to their own scripture too, to avoid any ranking of other traditions' texts. Confirm a Keeper agrees.
